power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Disordered eating (DE) can be particularly concerning during pregnancy, as it is associated with various obstetric complications.
Findings on DE variations during pregnancy have yet to be systematically synthesized.
This review seeks to summarize research on DE change across pregnancy.
Four databases were searched using PRISMA Scoping Review and Cochrane Rapid Reviews guidelines.
Eligible studies were longitudinal and assessed DE, including eating disorder (ED) symptoms (e.g., dieting, purging) and related forms of DE (e.g., emotional eating), more than once during pregnancy.
The review included 19 articles.
Though many forms of DE decreased across pregnancy, some forms of DE did not change, while some forms of DE had conflicting or unclear patterns.
Body image constructs were the most examined forms of DE in pregnancy, followed by weight and dieting constructs.
Research comparing DE patterns in people with versus without EDs was scarce.
Few studies have examined DE across pregnancy using ED samples, and several DE symptoms had conflicting or unclear patterns across pregnancy.

Moreover, some DE outcomes (e.g., quality of life related to EDs, guilt related to overeating, susceptibility to hunger) and the comparison of DE patterns in samples with versus without EDs remain underexplored in pregnancy.

Disordered eating (DE) refers to a wide range of unhelpful and unhealthy cognitions and behaviours related to eating that may negatively affect one's emotional, social, and physical well-being (APA, 2013; National Eating Disorders Collaboration, 2015; Bannatyne et al., 2018).

text.text: DE is not limited to individuals who meet Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) criteria for eating disorders (EDs) and may occur across the population at different rates and intensities (Reba-Harrelson et al., 2009; Wells et al., 2020).

text.text: Understanding how certain forms of DE may change across pregnancy is crucial, as it may improve screening efforts and allow for earlier and more targeted interventions for DE in this time-limited period.
Past research on changes in DE during pregnancy shows mixed findings in both ED and non-ED samples.

In women with current or past EDs, some studies report decreases in symptoms across pregnancy (Easter et al., 2015), while others found symptom worsening or relapse (Makino et al., 2020; Sommerfeldt et al., 2022).

Trajectories may not only vary across different types of DE but may also depend on individual characteristics (e.g., ED diagnosis status).

text.text: We conducted a rapid scoping review to map the existing literature and provide an overview of knowledge on variation in DE across different stages of pregnancy.

This rapid scoping review aimed to identify: (1) changes in different forms of DE that have been studied across pregnancy, and (2) differences in changes in DE across pregnancy in people with and without EDs.

We hypothesized articles would mostly find lower levels of DE from early to mid-pregnancy but moderately higher levels toward late pregnancy, and that this general pattern in DE would be found in both samples with and without EDs.

To ensure rigour and replicability of this rapid scoping review, we followed guidelines set by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI), the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR), as well as the Cochrane Rapid Reviews Methods (Peters et al., 2020; Tricco et al., 2018; Garritty et al., 2021).

text.text: Baseline DE assessments were conducted between conception and 27.8 weeks of pregnancy, and final assessments between the 28th week of pregnancy and delivery.

Given that most studies reported average change instead of patterns between time-point or trimesters, only general trajectories of change for DE found across first measure to last measure in pregnancy are discussed in the results.
Most studies used questionnaires (k = 14), whereas others used interviews (k = 3), both methods (k = 1), or a single Likertstyle item (k = 1).
The EDE, including its questionnaire version, the EDE-Q, was the most common tool (k = 7).

Across studies, five measured general DE scores (e.g., EDE-Q Global Score), nine examined body image (e.g., shape concerns, body dissatisfaction, negative attitudes about changes in appearance, feeling fat, preoccupation with size), seven assessed weight-related constructs (e.g., weight concerns, negative attitudes about change in weight during pregnancy, weight control via supplement use), seven assessed dieting-related constructs (e.g., dietary restraint, dietary restriction, dieting), and a smaller number examined binge eating (k = 4), purging (k = 4), eating concerns (including risk of orthorexia nervosa; k = 4), and emotional eating (k = 2).

Constructs such as quality of life related to EDs, overeating, hedonic hunger, loss of control over eating, susceptibility to hunger, disinhibition, and feelings of guilt related to overeating were each only assessed in one study.

Five studies used only descriptive methods (e.g., narrative summaries, graphs, and/or tables) to report changes in some or all forms of DE assessed across pregnancy (Easter et al., 2015; Emery et al., 2021; Lacey & Smith, 1987; Morgan et al., 1999; Nansel et al., 2020).

text.text: All 19 studies included in this review had their methodological quality assessed using the NIH Quality Assessment Tool for Observational Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies (National Institute of Health, 2021).
The score was calculated out of 11 for the included studies.
Seven of 19 (37%) were rated as fair, while twelve (63%) were rated as good.

This rapid scoping review aimed to summarize findings on DE during pregnancy and to identify gaps in research regarding: (1) changes in different forms of DE that have been studied across pregnancy and (2) differences between individuals with and without EDs.

Many forms of DE generally decreased across pregnancy, including general DE, dieting constructs, body image constructs, emotional eating, quality of life related to EDs, guilt related to overeating, and overeating.
Weight-related constructs showed conflicting patterns across studies, while disinhibition and susceptibility to hunger appeared unchanged (though these constructs were examined in only one study).

Changes in eating concerns, binge eating, purging behaviours, loss of control eating, and hedonic hunger were mostly or only examined descriptively; thus, their pattern of change across pregnancy remains unclear.
Body imagerelated constructs were the most frequently examined, followed by weight-and dieting-related constructs.
Only two studies compared ED and non-ED groups (Coker et al., 2013; Easter et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Only two studies compared ED and non-ED groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Coker et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Easter et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: They found that people with EDs reported improved quality of life and decreased general DE, whereas those without EDs experienced no change in quality of life but increases in DE, across pregnancy.
Studies including only ED samples and studies including only non-ED samples mostly reported decreases in DE across pregnancy.
However, methodological differences were apparent: ED-only studies were generally older, descriptive, and retrospective, while studies of non-ED samples used more varied approaches.
The general pattern of decrease in DE during pregnancy may reflect shifts in priorities toward infant health and changing social expectations during pregnancy (Clark et al., 2009).

text.text: A systematic review found that pregnant women often prioritize infant well-being over body image and tend to view bodily changes as natural and indicative of healthy pregnancy progression (Watson et al., 2015).

text.text: Decreases in DE during pregnancy may also relate to fluctuations in ovarian hormones, particularly estradiol and progesterone.

Estradiol suppresses food intake, peaking during preovulation, while progesterone increases food intake in the presence of estradiol by attenuating its inhibitory effects (Eckel, 2011; Buffenstein et al., 1995; Baker et al., 2012; Pelkman et al., 2001).

text.text: As both hormones rise throughout pregnancy, their interaction, especially in late pregnancy, may reduce dietary restraint.

Supporting this, body dissatisfaction and drive for thinness have been shown to be inversely associated with estradiol and positively associated with progesterone in community samples (Racine et al., 2012).

text.text: However, studies in non-ED samples found no significant changes in susceptibility to hunger or disinhibition across pregnancy (Jacob et al., 2023; Bond et al., 2001; Plante et al., 2020).

text.text: Thus, the role of ovarian hormones in shaping specific DE symptoms during pregnancy remains unclear.
Future studies should examine hormone associations longitudinally across pregnancy, as existing work has focused on the menstrual cycle rather than pregnancy.
Weight-related constructs (i.e., weight concerns, negative attitudes about change in weight during pregnancy, weight control behaviours) demonstrated conflicting patterns of change during pregnancy.
While variability in patterns may be attributed to differences in tools used to measure these constructs, sociocultural factors may also be at play.

For instance, generational shifts in body weight perceptions across time could explain why Fairburn et al. (1992) found an increase in weight-related concerns across pregnancy, as opposed to the decrease or unchanged pattern found in more recent studies (Lu et al., 2015; Burke et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2008).

text.text: In addition, the increases in weightrelated concerns across pregnancy found in Yamamiya & Omori (2023) may reflect the greater pervasiveness of the thinness ideal in Japanese society compared to Western society (Wardle et al., 2006).

text.text: Thus, generational and cultural differences in body weight perception may influence the pattern of change in specific DE symptoms.
Eating concerns, binge eating, purging behaviours, loss of control over eating, and hedonic hunger had unclear patterns of change given that they were mostly or only examined via descriptive methods.
Thus, future studies should aim to replicate findings using statistical testing to verify the significance of these changes.

text.text: However, comparisons across studies was challenging for several reasons: (1) heterogenous analytic approaches, ranging from descriptive reporting to varied inferential methods; (2) lack of standardized effect sizes, which made it difficult to assess the magnitude of change in DE across pregnancy; (3) initial and final measures of DE being taken at different ranges of weeks gestation; ( 4) lack of reporting of patterns of changes between trimesters specifically (as most studies only reported the overall pattern across pregnancy, even if they had more than two measures); and (5) most studies did not report whether levels of DE endorsement were above or below clinical cut-offs.

text.text: Based on the limitations and gaps identified in this review, future studies should use samples consisting of both people with and without EDs to not only replicate findings and assess a broader spectrum of DE outcomes in pregnancy, but also to clarify the patterns of change of the forms of DE that were found to be conflicting or unclear.
In addition, researchers should also report whether DE scores go above or below clinical cut-off through timepoints.

Studies should also prioritize effect size reporting, standardization of assessment timepoints during pregnancy, and meta-analytic approaches to improve reliability, generalizability, and clinical relevance.
Findings support that DE may affect pregnant women regardless of ED status and that it is highly heterogenous presentation-wise.
Treatments should thus be tailored to the specific type of DE being endorsed, as well as the person's ED status or ED history.

This review also shows that not all forms of DE follow the same pattern through time, as some may have higher levels of endorsement early during pregnancy, while some may sustain a stable level throughout trimesters.
Thus, DE support should be continuous throughout pregnancy, with supplementary support being provided during periods where DE endorsement is higher.
This rapid scoping review aimed to summarize broad patterns of change in DE symptoms across pregnancy and differences between people with and without EDs.
Most studies reported decreases in DE throughout pregnancy.
Body image constructs were the most examined outcomes.

Though some differences in general DE and quality of life related to EDs emerged between ED and non-ED groups, additional research is needed to determine the robustness and clinical significance of these findings.

text.text:  Some DE outcomes, such as total DE scores, dieting constructs, body image constructs, emotional eating, quality of life related to EDs, guilt related to overeating, and overeating were found to broadly decrease across pregnancy, while some were found to have conflicting patterns (e.g., weight-related constructs, binge eating, purging behaviours) or unclear patterns (e.g., eating concerns, loss of control eating, hedonic hunger).
 Body image constructs were the most frequently examined forms of DE across pregnancy, followed by weight-related and dieting-related constructs.

 Literature comparing DE patterns in pregnancy between people with and without EDs remains scarce, as only two studies examined these differences in DE patterns across pregnancy between these two populations.
